items.note: Blackwell datacenter GPU; DGX B200 packages eight of them as the standard enterprise training node

items.note: Rack-scale system pairing 36 Grace CPUs with 72 Blackwell GPUs on a single NVLink domain; the flagship AI training platform of the Blackwell generation

items.name: H200
items.note: Hopper-generation GPU with 141GB HBM3e; the volume inference and training part that preceded Blackwell

reading.body:
The six accelerators catalogued here represent the realistic hardware menu for large-scale AI workloads as of mid-2026: three from NVIDIA spanning two generations, two from AMD, and one from Intel.

The NVIDIA entries illustrate a clear architectural progression. The H200 established HBM3e memory as the volume standard for inference and training. The B200 and the GB200 NVL72 then scaled that foundation upward, with the NVL72 moving the unit of deployment from a single server to a 72-GPU rack bound by a single NVLink domain. That shift matters for buildings and power: a rack-scale system is a power and cooling commitment measured in tens of kilowatts per unit, not a decision made at the server level. AMD's MI350 series answers with 288GB HBM3E per part, the largest memory figure in this set, and is positioned explicitly against Blackwell. Intel's Gaudi 3 differs structurally by using Ethernet for scale-out rather than a proprietary interconnect, which has implications for how a datacenter is wired but the data does not quantify that difference in throughput or cost.

What this data does not cover: actual throughput numbers, pricing, availability volumes, or power draw figures for any of the six parts. It establishes which products exist and who makes them, and it records that AMD achieved meaningful LLM inference adoption at scale with the MI300 series, a notable competitive development. It does not say how market share is distributed across the six, or whether supply of any part is the current binding constraint on AI capacity.
